newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Albright arrives in S. Korea to discuss peace efforts.
newsitem.headline: Albright arrives in S. Korea to discuss peace efforts.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright turned her attention from Europe to Asia on Saturday, arriving in Seoul for meetings with South Korean officials that could lead to preliminary peace talks with the North.

North Korea said on Friday that it would attend a briefing with the United States and South Korea on Korean peace talks, a sign the communist North was trying to put on a normal face after an embarrassing high-level defection.
In a brief statement by the Foreign Ministry, Pyongyang said it would attend the U.S.-South Korean briefing in New York on March 5 to discuss four-way peace talks involving China.
U.S. officials, burned twice before when Pyongyang scheduled and then cancelled the briefing, hoped the announcement was genuine but were cautious in their public remarks.
"I cannot confirm that there is an agreement," State Department spokesman Nichols Burns said.

"The secretary of state needs to talk the South Korean government and we need to check back with the State Department in Washington on contacts with the North Koreans in New York," he told reporters on Albright's airplane arriving from Moscow.
"We have to get our ducks in a row," he said, but added that Albright "would like to work this out quickly."
Albright, beginning the Asian leg of a nine-nation world tour, was to meet South Korean President Kim Young-sam and Foreign Minister Yoo Chong.
She would then visit the demilitarized zone between North and South, where 37,000 U.S. troops help keep an uneasy peace that has existed since the 1950-53 Korean War.
On her first overseas trip since becoming secretary of state last month, Albright started off in Europe, aiming to put momentum and substance behind the NATO expansion effort.
But unlike her predecessors, she also insisted on including Asia on the trip "to make the statement that the United States is a global power, an Atlantic and Pacific power," Burns said.
North Korea delayed the peace talks "briefing" earlier this month and late January in what was seen as an effort to press Washington to provide more food aid for its hungry population.
Washington insists it never promised Pyongyang a specific amount of food aid in return for the Stalinist regime's participation in the briefing.
But Pyongyang reneged on its promise to attend earlier briefings when it was unable to close a deal with U.S.-based Cargill Inc. on 500,000 tonnes of grain.

This week, however, the United States and South Korea acted to alleviate the North's food needs by pledging $10 million and $6 million in new assistance, respectively, through the World Food Programme, a United Nations agency.
The four-way talks were proposed last April by Washington and Seoul to defuse tensions -- and eventually bring about a permanent peace -- on the Korean peninsula.
The two Koreas have remained technically at war since the 1950-53 conflict ended in a truce and not a peace pact.

Albright is also expected to discuss with South Korean leaders the 1994 U.S.-North Korean accord under which Pyongyang agreed to freeze its nuclear programme in return for $5 billion in light-water nuclear power reactors and alternative energy.
Burns said the United States "has no doubt that the freeze is still on."

Albright and South Korean officials are also expected to discuss Hwang Jang-yop, a close adviser to North Korean leader Kim Jong-il who defected to the South Korean embassy in Beijing on February 12. Washington has urged North and South Korea and China to resolve the row peacefully.
On Friday, North Korea announced the appointment of an acting premier to replace Kang Song-san, the sixth-ranked official in its power structure.
The news set off new speculation about turmoil in North Korea's leadership since Hwang Jang-yop's defection.

On Saturday North Korea's official radio reported that Defence Minister Choe Kwang had died of a heart attack at 78. No other details were immediately available on the senior official or who would be named to replace him in the powerful post.
